name: Pedro Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader at Stonebank mine and carry ore from the face to the transfer point. I have a vocational certificate and fifteen years on heavy machines, though I am no engineer. My partner and I have grown children and enough saved for more than six months. I try an AI app now and then to read equipment notices, after someone else has checked it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker form is fine if it leaves the loader work alone. I have seen plenty of promising screens come and go. The tyres, brakes and face still need checking by a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage looks safe, and our savings and nearby mines give us room if something goes wrong. I might use the app for notices a bit more, but I would not change how I check a machine. Retirement is near enough to keep the pension figures in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my loader shifts and do the same pre-start walk. In the first year I would ask payroll for a pension statement and sit with my partner to read it. I would use the notice app only after checking any advice against the mechanic’s note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The small change saves a little paper, and our household can pay its bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the notice app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mechanic’s note and the app agreed over a few months, I might read it first. I would still check the machine number. A wrong number on a brake notice can put the wrong loader on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why get the pension statement now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am fifty-eight, and the numbers matter whether AI grows or stalls. My partner likes to see the figures before we talk about a date. I do too.

say: I would accept **quicker forms** while drivers still inspect loaders and the mine face.
I would keep the **pre-start walk** on every shift.
think: My **wage** looks secure, with strong savings and other nearby mines.
I want **pension figures** before discussing a retirement date with my partner.
do: **Keep** driving the Stonebank loader and checking tyres and brakes.
**Request** a pension statement and review it with my partner this year.
S0.quote: A wrong number on a brake notice can put the wrong loader on the road.
fieldNote: He trusts **tested tools** but checks machine numbers and physical condition himself.
His **savings** and local job options support a calm mood in the plateau.
Retirement planning is driven by **age**, not only AI.

steps.text: Keep driving Stonebank loader and performing pre-start checks
Request pension statement before choosing retirement date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office will change before my loader seat does, because buying and planning happen on screens. I would ask for a trial of any new dispatch plan. The crew should see whether the target can be met on a wet road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours look reasonably safe while robots spread slowly. Still, I could see the mine not replacing a dispatcher and asking drivers to make up lost time. I would watch for shorter breaks rather than assume a new plan is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI dispatch screen from a colleague who has used it for a month. I would compare its load times with my own trip notes during a four-week trial. If breaks shrank, I would take the figures to the supervisor and ask for the target to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can manage a screen after it has been tested, but I do not want a desk target deciding road safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trip would prove the target wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The uphill run after rain takes longer with a full bucket. A dry-day average hides the extra braking distance. I would log that trip rather than argue from memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the supervisor ignored the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring it to the crew safety meeting with two other drivers. I have enough years here to speak plainly, but I would want their observations too. One bad target is fixable if people listen.

say: I would ask for a **dispatch trial** before new load targets take effect.
I would let **wet-road trips** count in the figures.
think: My **loader hours** look fairly safe while hands-on robots spread slowly.
A missing **dispatcher** could leave drivers with tighter targets and breaks.
do: **Learn** the AI dispatch screen from an experienced colleague.
**Compare** four weeks of load times with trip notes and raise shorter breaks.
feel: **Uneasy** about road safety under new targets.
S1.quote: A dry-day average hides the extra braking distance.
fieldNote: He accepts AI only after a **colleague tests it**, matching his steady adaptability.
He expects **desk changes** first and watches for indirect pressure on driver breaks.
The trial relies on **actual trip times** in wet conditions.

steps.text: Learn AI dispatch screen from colleague during first month
Bring shortened break records to crew safety meeting if ignored

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell drivers that thinking AI arrives by 2028 in this picture, while capable robot loaders come around 2031. The mine would still have to decide whether to buy them. I would ask management for a purchase plan and a clear account of any driver posts lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when planning work changes and sixty-three when capable robot loaders appear. If Stonebank bought them quickly, I might lose a high wage before I planned to retire. We have savings, but I would not assume they cover years without work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would delay replacing our car and check the mortgage and pension balances this month. I would keep driving after 2028 while the mine still needs operators. I would take paid instruction on remote loader checks if the mine posted real monitoring work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have time and money to make a plan, yet the 2031 truck yard is close enough to picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look only after seeing which mines are buying robot loaders. There are plenty nearby. A loader vacancy today says little about 2031. I would not sell our house on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make remote monitoring worth learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid course and a posted job, not a promise that somebody might be needed. I am comfortable learning a proven machine control. I would want the work terms in writing before changing my retirement plan.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable robot loaders around 2031.
I would ask for a **purchase plan** and clear numbers on any lost operator posts.
think: At **sixty-three** when capable robots appear, I could lose a high wage if Stonebank buys them.
Our **savings** help, but may not cover years without work.
do: **Delay** replacing the family car and review pension and mortgage balances.
**Take** paid remote loader instruction if a real monitoring job is posted.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the loader wage before planned retirement.
S2.quote: A loader vacancy today says little about 2031.
fieldNote: He separates the **thinking date** from later capable hands-on robots.
Savings give him choices, but a lost **high wage** at sixty-three would still matter.
Remote instruction is conditional on **paid training** and a posted monitoring job.

steps.text: Delay replacing the family car this year
Keep driving Stonebank loader after 2028 while operators remain
Take paid remote loader instruction if monitoring job is posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robot loaders gives the mine time to plan without rushing. I would ask for a schedule of equipment trials and driver training. A date on paper would help families make sensible choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three in 2031 and about sixty-six when robots become capable in 2034. I might be able to retire by then, depending on the pension statement and mortgage. If not, I could learn remote checks while still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would book a meeting with the pension adviser this year and take the figures home. I would spend one paid day learning the remote loader controls if Stonebank offered a real monitoring post. I would keep my current loader shifts while the trial ran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a route through it. Eight years gives us time to test the numbers and the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the adviser?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what our monthly income would be at sixty-five and sixty-seven. I would compare both figures with our bills, not just look at a lump sum. My partner would come with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the monitoring post is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and check the pension numbers again next year. Another mine might post a similar job, but I would apply only if I needed more years of wages. I would not train for a job that did not exist.

say: I would request an **equipment timetable** and driver training schedule before capable robots around 2034.
I would use **pension figures** to decide whether more years of wages are needed.
think: At about **sixty-six** when robots become capable, retirement might be possible if the figures work.
A **monitoring post** offers another route if wages are still needed.
do: **Meet** a pension adviser and compare monthly income with household bills.
**Train** on remote loader controls for a paid day if a real post is offered.
**Keep** loader shifts while equipment trials run.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to test retirement and work options.
S3.quote: I would not train for a job that did not exist.
fieldNote: The future ages are **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive.
He will try remote controls only with **paid time** and a real post.
His retirement confidence depends on **monthly income**, not the size of a lump sum.

steps.text: Meet pension adviser to compare monthly income with bills
Train on remote loader controls if paid real post offered
Keep current loader shifts while equipment trials run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years before thinking AI and about thirteen before capable robot loaders is enough time to publish a fair plan. The mine should tell crews when trials begin. I would expect the safety people to test machines on wet roads too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when robots become capable in 2039. I hope to be retired by then, and our savings make that plausible. I would still check the pension figures rather than promise a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the loader job for now and update my pension statement this year. I would show a junior driver my wet-road notes during a regular shift. I would review the retirement date with my partner after we saw our monthly income estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household, though I would worry about younger operators carrying long loans. A decade gives me room to leave work on our terms if the sums hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early because of the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a headline. I like the work, and I would look at income first. If the figures supported it, my partner and I might choose an earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pass on the wet-road notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A junior driver can learn where water sits before a machine takes the route. My wet-road notes are only part of a junior driver's lesson; I would ride along and show the wet loader bend. That would still matter while people drive.

say: I would ask Stonebank for a **published trial plan** before capable robots around 2039.
I would include **wet-road tests** in safety checks.
think: At about **seventy-one** when robots become capable, I may already be retired if pension figures allow.
Our **savings** give us room to choose a date rather than rush.
do: **Keep** driving while updating my pension statement this year.
**Show** a junior driver the wet-road bend during a regular shift.
feel: **Calm** about household income, with concern for younger operators.
S4.quote: My wet-road notes are only part of a junior driver's lesson; I would ride along and show the wet loader bend.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** falls near age seventy-one, when retirement is plausible but unconfirmed.
He favours **written trials** and passing road knowledge to younger drivers.
His mood is calm because **savings and options** support the household.

steps.text: Keep driving Stonebank loader on current shifts
Update pension statement before choosing retirement date
Show a junior loader driver wet-road notes during a regular shift

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot loaders could appear around 2031, before I know whether retirement works. A dated purchase plan and paid training tied to real monitoring posts would help. I would also need a reliable pension estimate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the mine tests robots on a wet road, not just a dry test pad. I have felt a loaded machine slide where a chart said the road was fine. I would want a driver in that trial.

headlineQuote: I have felt a loaded machine slide where a chart said the road was fine.
portrait: Pedro Silva is a **58-year-old** loader operator at Stonebank mine with a vocational certificate, a partner and grown children.
His **strong savings**, high wage and nearby mines give him options as retirement approaches.
He tries **proven tools** after colleagues do and checks new dispatch plans against wet-road driving times.
Fast capable robots make him **anxious** about losing wages before retirement; longer warning lets him test pension and monitoring options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robot loaders could appear around 2031 before retirement is settled.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated purchase plan**, paid instruction tied to monitoring posts and a reliable pension estimate would help.
